What Makes a Rural Crash Fatal or Seriously Injurious? A 10-Feature Logistic Regression¶

Question. Which factors contribute most to crashes in which someone is killed or suspected seriously injured (FATAL_OR_SUSP_SERIOUS_INJ) on rural roads?

Data. features.xls, an 80-column extract of PennDOT crash records (data dictionary: Crash_Data_Dictionary_2026.pdf).

Approach

Step What we do Section
Data cleaning Remove empty rows, collapse duplicated crash records, rebuild missing flags from source fields 2
Feature selection: first principles Keep only columns with a plausible physical or human mechanism of injury 3
Feature selection: filter Rank features by simple one-at-a-time statistics (Fisher's exact test, risk ratio), on all crashes and on rural crashes 4
Redundancy & final pick Collapse near-duplicate flags, then choose 10 features 5
Multicollinearity Correlation matrix and variance inflation factors (VIF) 6
Feature analysis How each feature relates to severity, overall and on rural roads 7
Final model Logistic regression: accuracy, precision, recall, F1 (overall and rural) 8

Rural lens. Only 11 of the 177 rural crashes were fatal or serious-injury, far too few to train a reliable 10-feature model on rural crashes alone. We therefore train on all crashes (36 severe outcomes) and apply a rural lens at every step:

  • the filter is run separately on rural crashes,
  • rural evidence is part of the final selection,
  • the model is evaluated on rural crashes on their own,
  • the conclusions are about rural roads.

Colors used throughout: ■ All crashes · ■ Rural crashes · ■ Highlight / selected

2. Data cleaning¶

2a. Remove empty rows¶

Rows 1000–1029 have no target and almost no data. Most contain only one or two flags; they are spreadsheet debris, not crashes.

In [3]:

      f"({debris.sum()} rows, index {debris.idxmax()}–{raw.index[debris][-1]})")

2b. Collapse duplicated crash records¶

The dictionary explains why crashes repeat. LANE_COUNT and SPEED_LIMIT come from the ROADWAY table, which can hold several rows per crash (one per road involved, RDWY_SEQ_NUM). When that table is joined to the crash data, a crash on two roads appears twice. The copies are identical except for the roadway fields and the randomly missing cells.

Rule: consecutive rows that agree on every non-roadway column where both have a value (at least 60 columns compared) are one crash.

Why it matters: without this step, the same crash can land in both the training and the test fold, which inflates every metric. It would also count each severe crash 2–5 times.

In [4]:
ROADWAY_COLS = ["LANE_COUNT", "SPEED_LIMIT"]
CRASH_COLS = [c for c in df.columns if c not in ROADWAY_COLS]

def same_crash(i, j):
    a, b = df.loc[i, CRASH_COLS], df.loc[j, CRASH_COLS]
    both = a.notna() & b.notna()
    return both.sum() >= 60 and (a[both] == b[both]).all()

crash_id = [0]
for i in range(1, len(df)):
    crash_id.append(crash_id[-1] if same_crash(i - 1, i) else crash_id[-1] + 1)
df["CRASH_ID"] = crash_id

sizes = df.groupby("CRASH_ID").size()
multi = df[df.CRASH_ID.isin(sizes[sizes > 1].index)]
evidence = pd.DataFrame({
    "Value": [len(df), df.CRASH_ID.nunique(), int((sizes > 1).sum()),
              int((multi.groupby("CRASH_ID")["TIME_OF_DAY"].nunique() > 1).sum()),
              int((multi.groupby("CRASH_ID")[ROADWAY_COLS].nunique().max(axis=1) > 1).sum())]},
    index=["Rows", "Distinct crashes", "Crashes recorded more than once",
           "…of which have conflicting TIME_OF_DAY (should be 0)",
           "…of which differ in SPEED_LIMIT / LANE_COUNT (multiple roads)"])
display(evidence)

2c. Missing values: rebuild what can be rebuilt¶

About 16 columns have ~20% randomly scattered gaps. Several of them are calculated flags whose source fields are complete, so they can be rebuilt exactly. Each rule is checked against every cell where the flag is known:

Flag Rebuilt from Dictionary basis
WET_ROAD ROAD_CONDITION is 08 (Water) or 09 (Wet) Roadway surface condition codes
YOUNG_DRIVER any DRIVER_COUNT_16YR … _20YR > 0 "at least 1 driver age 16–20"
DRIVER_20YR DRIVER_COUNT_20YR > 0 "at least one driver 20 years of age"
DRIVER_50_64YR DRIVER_COUNT_50_64YR > 0 "at least one driver 50–64"
MULTIPLE_VEHICLE VEHICLE_COUNT ≥ 2 "crash involved at least 2 vehicles"

    "WET_ROAD":         crash["ROAD_CONDITION"].isin([8, 9]),
    "YOUNG_DRIVER":     crash[[f"DRIVER_COUNT_{a}YR" for a in range(16, 21)]].sum(axis=1) > 0,
    "DRIVER_20YR":      crash["DRIVER_COUNT_20YR"] > 0,

for col, rule in RULES.items():

How the remaining gaps are handled

  • TIME_OF_DAY and ILLUMINATION duplicate complete columns (HOUR_OF_DAY and ILLUMINATION_DARK), so they are dropped.
  • CRASH_MONTH and DAY_OF_WEEK are calendar fields with no direct injury mechanism and are excluded in section 3.
  • Any other gap that remains in a feature used by the model is filled with the training-fold mean inside the model pipeline. The earlier missing-data notebook found mean imputation to be the least biased simple method, and computing the mean inside each fold avoids leakage.

3. Feature selection, step 1: first principles¶

Crash severity comes down to how much energy reaches a human body, and how well that body tolerates it. That gives a short list of mechanisms. Every column is assigned to one, or rejected if it has no direct mechanism:

Mechanism Reasoning Example columns
Energy / speed Kinetic energy grows with speed², so faster crashes transfer more energy SPEEDING, SPEED_LIMIT, INTERSTATE
Unprotected road user Motorcyclists and pedestrians have no crash structure, belts or airbags MOTORCYCLE, PEDESTRIAN, BICYCLE
Crash geometry Head-on and side impacts have high closing speeds and little crush space; rear-ends do not REAR_END, HEAD_ON, ANGLE, NON_COLLISION
Driver impairment & behavior Impaired, aggressive or distracted driving changes speeds, reaction times and crash types IMPAIRED_DRIVER, AGGRESSIVE_DRIVING, DISTRACTED
Occupant frailty / inexperience Older bodies tolerate less force; young drivers misjudge risk DRIVER_75PLUS, YOUNG_DRIVER
Environment Darkness and surface conditions change visibility, speed and friction ILLUMINATION_DARK, WET_ROAD, ICY_ROAD
Road setting Road class and traffic control shape speeds and conflicts STATE_ROAD, INTERSECTION, WORK_ZONE
Vehicle mix / exposure Heavier vehicles and more people raise the chance of a severe outcome HEAVY_TRUCK_COUNT, PERSON_COUNT, VEHICLE_COUNT

Rejected (no injury mechanism, an administrative field, or a duplicate of another column): county, month, day of week, the undocumented URBAN_AREA, and duplicated codes. RURAL is also not a candidate predictor, because it is the lens we analyze through: on rural roads it is constant, so it cannot explain which rural crashes become severe. Leakage check: no remaining column records the injury outcome itself (e.g. INJURY_COUNT, FATAL_COUNT), so none of them leaks the answer.

4. Feature selection, step 2: a simple filter¶

Each candidate is tested on its own against the outcome, with no model involved:

  • 0/1 flags: the severe rate when the flag is yes vs. no, as a risk ratio (RR = rate if yes ÷ rate if no), with Fisher's exact test (suitable for small counts).
  • Counts and numbers (SPEED_LIMIT, PERSON_COUNT, …): a Mann–Whitney test comparing severe and non-severe crashes.

Each test is run twice: on all crashes and on rural crashes only. A feature passes the filter if it is exposed in at least 15 crashes and has p < 0.20 in either group. The threshold is loose on purpose: this is a screening step, and with only 36 severe crashes a strict cut-off would discard real effects.

In [10]:
def univariate(d, col):
    s, t = d[col], d[TARGET]
    ok = s.notna()
    if crash[col].dropna().isin([0, 1]).all():
        a = int(((s == 1) & (t == 1)).sum()); n1 = int((s == 1).sum())
        b = int(((s == 0) & (t == 1)).sum()); n0 = int((s == 0).sum())
        if n1 == 0 or n0 == 0:
            return dict(n_exposed=n1, severe_exposed=a, rate_yes=np.nan, rate_no=np.nan, RR=np.nan, p=np.nan)
        p = fisher_exact([[a, n1 - a], [b, n0 - b]])[1]
        rr = (a / n1) / (b / n0) if b else np.nan
        return dict(n_exposed=n1, severe_exposed=a, rate_yes=a / n1, rate_no=b / n0, RR=rr, p=p)
    p = mannwhitneyu(s[ok & (t == 1)], s[ok & (t == 0)])[1]
    return dict(n_exposed=int(ok.sum()), severe_exposed=int(t[ok].sum()), rate_yes=s[ok & (t == 1)].mean(),
                rate_no=s[ok & (t == 0)].mean(), RR=np.nan, p=p)

rural_crash = crash[crash.RURAL == 1]
flt = pd.concat({
    "All crashes": pd.DataFrame({c: univariate(crash, c) for c in CANDIDATES}).T,
    "Rural crashes": pd.DataFrame({c: univariate(rural_crash, c) for c in CANDIDATES}).T}, axis=1)
flt.insert(0, ("", "Mechanism"), [mech_of[c] for c in flt.index])
flt[("", "Passes filter")] = ((flt[("All crashes", "n_exposed")] >= 15) &
                              ((flt[("All crashes", "p")] < 0.20) | (flt[("Rural crashes", "p")] < 0.20)))
flt = flt.sort_values(("All crashes", "p"))

def fmt_rr(v): return "" if pd.isna(v) else ("0 severe" if v == 0 else f"{v:.2f}")

is_flag = {c: crash[c].dropna().isin([0, 1]).all() for c in flt.index}
def fmt_rate(v, c): return "" if pd.isna(v) else (f"{v:.1%}" if is_flag[c] else f"mean {v:.2f}")
show = pd.DataFrame(index=flt.index)
show["Mechanism"] = flt[("", "Mechanism")]
for scope in ["All crashes", "Rural crashes"]:
    show[(scope, "Exposed (yes)")] = [f"{int(flt.loc[c, (scope, 'n_exposed')])}" if is_flag[c] else "numeric" for c in flt.index]
    show[(scope, "Severe if yes")] = [fmt_rate(flt.loc[c, (scope, "rate_yes")], c) for c in flt.index]
    show[(scope, "Severe if no")] = [fmt_rate(flt.loc[c, (scope, "rate_no")], c) for c in flt.index]
    show[(scope, "Risk ratio")] = flt[(scope, "RR")].map(fmt_rr)
    show[(scope, "p")] = flt[(scope, "p")].astype(float)
show["Passes filter"] = flt[("", "Passes filter")].map({True: "✔ yes", False: ""})
show.columns = pd.MultiIndex.from_tuples([c if isinstance(c, tuple) else ("", c) for c in show.columns])
(show.style.format("{:.3f}", subset=[c for c in show.columns if c[1] == "p"], na_rep="")
     .map(lambda v: "background-color: #f4c7c3" if v < 0.05 else ("background-color: #fbe5d6" if v < 0.20 else ""),
          subset=[c for c in show.columns if c[1] == "p"])
     .map(lambda v: "font-weight: bold; color: #1c5cab" if v else "", subset=[("", "Passes filter")])
     .set_caption("Univariate filter for every candidate, sorted by all-crash p-value. For numeric features "
                  "('mean'), the two rate columns show the mean in severe vs. non-severe crashes"))

5. Feature selection, step 3: remove redundancy and choose the final 10¶

Several flags that pass the filter are the same information under different names: one flag is a subset of another, or the two are identical. Keeping both splits one effect across two coefficients and causes multicollinearity. The table below measures the overlap directly, as the share of crashes with flag A that also have flag B.

In [12]:
PAIRS = [("DRINKING_DRIVER", "ALCOHOL_RELATED"), ("DRINKING_DRIVER", "IMPAIRED_DRIVER"),
         ("RUNNING_STOP_SIGN", "AGGRESSIVE_DRIVING"), ("RUNNING_RED_LT", "AGGRESSIVE_DRIVING"),
         ("SPEEDING", "AGGRESSIVE_DRIVING"), ("SUDDEN_DEER", "DEER_RELATED"),
         ("DRIVER_75PLUS", "MATURE_DRIVER"), ("WORK_ZONE", "WORK_ZONE_IND"), ("PEDESTRIAN", "VULNERABLE_ROAD_USER")]
ov = []
for a, b in PAIRS:
    A, B = crash[a] == 1, crash[b] == 1
    ov.append({"Flag A": a, "Flag B": b, "Crashes with A": int(A.sum()), "% of A that are also B": (A & B).sum() / A.sum(),
               "% of B that are also A": (A & B).sum() / B.sum(), "phi correlation": crash[[a, b]].corr().iloc[0, 1]})
(pd.DataFrame(ov).style.format({"% of A that are also B": "{:.0%}", "% of B that are also A": "{:.0%}", "phi correlation": "{:.2f}"})
   .bar(subset=["% of A that are also B"], color="#b7d3f6", vmin=0, vmax=1).hide(axis="index")
   .set_caption("Overlap between related flags"))

Redundancy decisions

  • ALCOHOL_RELATED = DRINKING_DRIVER (identical), and both sit inside IMPAIRED_DRIVER → keep the umbrella IMPAIRED_DRIVER.
  • RUNNING_STOP_SIGN and RUNNING_RED_LT are 100% inside AGGRESSIVE_DRIVING (PennDOT counts them as aggressive actions) → keep AGGRESSIVE_DRIVING.
  • SPEEDING is also inside AGGRESSIVE_DRIVING, but it is kept as well. It has its own physical mechanism (energy), the strongest filter signal of any behavior, and the multicollinearity check in section 6 shows the pair is fine. With both in the model, AGGRESSIVE_DRIVING measures aggressive actions other than speeding.
  • SUDDEN_DEER ≈ DEER_RELATED → keep DEER_RELATED. DRIVER_COUNT_75PLUS ≈ DRIVER_75PLUS → keep the flag DRIVER_75PLUS.

Final pick. After merging those duplicates, the strongest features (ranked by all-crash p-value) are combined with first-principles strength and rural evidence:

6. Multicollinearity check¶

Two diagnostics:

  • Correlation matrix (phi coefficient, the Pearson correlation for 0/1 flags). Values above ~0.7 would signal trouble.
  • Variance inflation factor (VIF): how much a coefficient's variance is inflated by overlap with the other features. Rule of thumb: VIF > 5 is a concern, VIF > 10 a serious problem.

For contrast, we also compute the VIFs for the set of flags that would have been chosen without removing redundancy.

In [15]:
X_final = crash[FINAL].astype(float)
corr = X_final.corr()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 7))
mask = np.triu(np.ones_like(corr, dtype=bool))
sns.heatmap(corr, mask=mask, annot=True, fmt=".2f", cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-1, vmax=1, center=0, square=True,
            linewidths=2, linecolor="white", cbar_kws={"shrink": 0.7, "label": "phi correlation"}, ax=ax,
            annot_kws={"fontsize": 8})
ax.set_title("Correlation between the 10 selected features"); ax.grid(False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print(f"Largest absolute correlation: {corr.where(~np.eye(len(corr), dtype=bool)).abs().max().max():.2f}")

Largest absolute correlation: 0.29
In [16]:
def vif_table(cols):
    X = sm.add_constant(crash[cols].astype(float).fillna(crash[cols].mean()))
    return pd.Series([variance_inflation_factor(X.values, i) for i in range(1, X.shape[1])], index=cols)

naive = ["REAR_END", "MOTORCYCLE", "AGGRESSIVE_DRIVING", "SPEEDING", "DISTRACTED", "IMPAIRED_DRIVER",
         "DRINKING_DRIVER", "ALCOHOL_RELATED", "RUNNING_STOP_SIGN", "DRIVER_COUNT_75PLUS"]
v_final, v_naive = vif_table(FINAL), vif_table(naive)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 4.2), sharex=False)
for ax, v, title, color in [(axes[0], v_final, "Selected 10 features", C_ALL),
                            (axes[1], v_naive.clip(upper=30), "Top 10 by p-value WITHOUT removing redundancy", C_GRAY)]:
    v = v.sort_values()
    ax.barh(v.index, v.values, color=[C_HI if x > 5 else color for x in v.values], edgecolor="white", height=0.7)
    for i, (name, x) in enumerate(v.items()):
        lbl = "∞ (identical columns)" if (title.startswith("Top") and v_naive[name] > 1e6) else f"{x:.2f}"
        ax.text(x + 0.2, i, lbl, va="center", fontsize=8, color="#52514e")
    ax.axvline(5, color="#c98500", lw=1, ls="--"); ax.axvline(10, color="#e34948", lw=1, ls="--")
    ax.set_title(title); ax.set_xlabel("VIF  (dashed: 5 = concern, 10 = serious)")
    ax.set_xlim(0, 33 if title.startswith("Top") else 12); ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Result: every VIF for the selected 10 is close to 1 (the largest is ~1.24), and the largest correlation is 0.29, well below any warning level. That pair is ILLUMINATION_DARK with IMPAIRED_DRIVER, since impaired driving happens mostly at night. The model can separate each feature's effect. The naive set, without redundancy removal, contains identical columns (ALCOHOL_RELATED = DRINKING_DRIVER), whose VIF is infinite. The redundancy step in section 5 was necessary.

6a. Association tests: Pearson (continuous) and chi-square (categorical)¶

The correlation matrix and VIF above check the final model. As a second, pair-by-pair check, we also run the two association tests used for feature screening:

Variable types Test Strength measure
Two continuous / count variables Pearson correlation $r$ (from −1 to 1)
Two categorical (yes/no) variables Chi-square test on their contingency table Cramér's V (0 to 1; for two yes/no variables it equals |phi|)

How to read them.

  • The p-value answers "is there any association?". The null hypothesis is that the two variables are independent. A small p-value (e.g. < 0.05) means they are associated; a large one means no association was detected. With hundreds of crashes, even a trivial link can be "significant".
  • The strength ($|r|$ or V) answers "are they so similar that one is redundant?". Decision rule: above 0.8, drop one of the pair; 0.7–0.8 is marginal; below 0.7, keep both.

So a pair can be significantly associated and still both be kept, as long as the association is weak.

In [17]:
# Worked example: AGGRESSIVE_DRIVING x ALCOHOL_RELATED
from itertools import combinations
from scipy.stats import chi2_contingency, pearsonr

def assoc(a, b, d=crash):
    t = pd.crosstab(d[a], d[b])
    chi2, p, dof, expected = chi2_contingency(t, correction=False)
    v = np.sqrt(chi2 / (t.values.sum() * (min(t.shape) - 1)))
    p_exact = fisher_exact(t.values)[1] if t.shape == (2, 2) else np.nan
    return t, expected, chi2, p, v, p_exact

def verdict(s):
    return "Drop one (> 0.8)" if s > 0.8 else ("Marginal (0.7–0.8)" if s >= 0.7 else "Keep both (< 0.7)")

t, expected, chi2, p, v, _ = assoc("AGGRESSIVE_DRIVING", "ALCOHOL_RELATED")
lab = {0: "No", 1: "Yes"}
obs = t.rename(index=lab, columns=lab).rename_axis(index="Aggressive driving", columns="Alcohol related")
exp = pd.DataFrame(expected, index=obs.index, columns=obs.columns).round(1)
display(pd.concat({"Observed crashes": obs, "Expected if independent": exp}, axis=1)
          .style.set_caption("Contingency table: aggressive driving x alcohol"))
print(f"Chi-square = {chi2:.2f}, df = 1, p = {p:.3f}, Cramér's V = {v:.2f}")
print(f"→ p < 0.05: the two ARE associated (alcohol crashes are less often aggressive than independence predicts),")
print(f"  but V = {v:.2f} is far below 0.7, so the association is weak → {verdict(v).lower()}.")

Association-test results

  • Pearson: only VEHICLE_COUNT and TOTAL_UNITS exceed 0.8 (r ≈ 0.97: total units = vehicles + pedestrians/cyclists, almost the same number). One of them would have to go, but neither is in the final ten (crash geometry is captured more directly by the collision-type flags). Every other numeric pair is well below 0.7.
  • Chi-square among the final ten: many pairs are statistically associated (p < 0.05), as expected for crash characteristics that co-occur. Examples: impaired driving with darkness, rear-ends with distraction. But every Cramér's V is ≤ 0.29, far below 0.7. Each feature carries distinct information, so all ten are kept, which agrees with the VIF result.
  • Redundant pairs from section 5: the tests confirm those decisions. Five pairs have V above 0.8: DRINKING_DRIVER × ALCOHOL_RELATED (1.00), WORK_ZONE × WORK_ZONE_IND (1.00), SUDDEN_DEER × DEER_RELATED (0.99), PEDESTRIAN × VULNERABLE_ROAD_USER (0.92) and DRINKING_DRIVER × IMPAIRED_DRIVER (0.88). In each case only one flag, or neither, is in the final ten; we kept the umbrella flags IMPAIRED_DRIVER and DEER_RELATED. DRIVER_75PLUS × MATURE_DRIVER (0.63) is below the threshold, and only DRIVER_75PLUS was selected. The subset relationships (RUNNING_STOP_SIGN ⊂ AGGRESSIVE_DRIVING) have a low V, which is why they were removed for nesting, not for correlation: the overlap table in section 5 shows that 100% of stop-sign crashes are aggressive-driving crashes.
  • Small expected counts: chi-square is unreliable when an expected cell count is below 5 (common for rare flags such as MOTORCYCLE). Fisher's exact test is reported alongside for those pairs.

What stands out

  • Deer crashes are distinctly rural. About one in six rural crashes involves a deer, versus one in twenty-five elsewhere (4× more common), and none of them was severe. Non-collision events (rollovers, etc.), which raise severity, are also ~3× more common on rural roads.
  • The main risk factors are about as common on rural roads as elsewhere. Aggressive driving appears in about half of all crashes in both settings, and impairment, speeding and drivers aged 75+ in similar shares. Rural crashes are not more often aggressive or impaired; those factors simply matter just as much there.
  • Rear-end and distraction crashes are about half as common on rural roads (they come with traffic and congestion). They are the clearest low-severity markers, which helps explain why rural crashes are slightly more often severe (6.2% vs. 5.0%).

7b. Why is darkness protective here?¶

First principles say darkness should make crashes more severe, yet in this sample dark crashes are severe less often. The table below shows why:

In this sample, motorcycle crashes (the most dangerous type) happen almost entirely in daylight (4.5% of daylight crashes vs. 0.7% of dark ones), and dark crashes are twice as often deer strikes (12% vs. 6%, never severe here). Dark crashes are more often single-vehicle and impaired, but those did not outweigh the missing motorcycle crashes. Darkness itself is not protective: it marks a different mix of crashes. Even so, it is a useful predictor. The model keeps it, and we interpret it as "dark-condition crash types are less severe in this data", not as "darkness makes roads safer". With only 5 severe dark crashes, this pattern could also be chance.

8. The final model¶

Setup

  • Model: logistic regression on the 10 selected features. Mean imputation for the few remaining gaps (only MOTORCYCLE has any) and standardization are both learned inside each training fold. A mild L2 penalty is used, because REAR_END, DEER_RELATED and DISTRACTED have zero severe crashes: an unpenalized model would push their coefficients to minus infinity.
  • Class imbalance: only 5.3% of crashes are severe. A model that always predicts "not severe" scores 94.7% accuracy and an F1 of 0, so we weight the classes (class_weight="balanced").
  • Decision threshold: the cut-off that converts a probability into a "severe" prediction is tuned to maximize F1. It is chosen inside each training fold (by an inner cross-validation), so the test fold never influences it.
  • Evaluation: stratified 5-fold cross-validation, repeated 20 times (100 test folds). We report mean ± standard deviation for all crashes and for rural crashes only. With only 36 severe crashes, a single train/test split would be unreliable.
In [24]:
def make_model(C=1.0):
    return make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(strategy="mean"), StandardScaler(),
                         LogisticRegression(C=C, class_weight="balanced", max_iter=5000))

def best_f1_threshold(y_true, prob):
    prec, rec, thr = precision_recall_curve(y_true, prob)
    f1 = 2 * prec * rec / np.clip(prec + rec, 1e-12, None)
    return thr[np.nanargmax(f1[:-1])]

def evaluate(cols, n_repeats=20, seed=42):
    # Repeated CV with a nested (inner-CV) F1-optimal threshold; returns per-fold metrics and out-of-fold probabilities
    X = crash[cols].astype(float).values
    outer = RepeatedStratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, n_repeats=n_repeats, random_state=seed)
    recs, oof = [], np.full((n_repeats, len(y)), np.nan)
    thresholds = []
    for k, (tr, te) in enumerate(outer.split(X, y)):
        inner_prob = cross_val_predict(make_model(), X[tr], y[tr], cv=StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=k),
                                       method="predict_proba")[:, 1]
        thr = best_f1_threshold(y[tr], inner_prob); thresholds.append(thr)
        prob = make_model().fit(X[tr], y[tr]).predict_proba(X[te])[:, 1]
        oof[k // 5, te] = prob
        pred = (prob >= thr).astype(int)
        for scope, m in [("All crashes", np.ones(len(te), bool)), ("Rural crashes", is_rural[te])]:
            yt, yp, pp = y[te][m], pred[m], prob[m]
            recs.append({"scope": scope, "fold": k, "Accuracy": accuracy_score(yt, yp),
                         "Precision": precision_score(yt, yp, zero_division=0), "Recall": recall_score(yt, yp, zero_division=0),
                         "F1": f1_score(yt, yp, zero_division=0),
                         "ROC AUC": roc_auc_score(yt, pp) if 0 < yt.sum() < len(yt) else np.nan})
    return pd.DataFrame(recs), oof, np.array(thresholds)

folds, oof, thresholds = evaluate(FINAL)
print(f"Tuned decision threshold: median {np.median(thresholds):.2f} (range {thresholds.min():.2f}–{thresholds.max():.2f})")

Tuned decision threshold: median 0.75 (range 0.56–0.88)

thr = np.median(thresholds)
pred0 = (prob0 >= thr).astype(int)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.3))
for ax, (scope, m, cmap) in zip(axes, [("All crashes", np.ones(len(y), bool), "Blues"), ("Rural crashes", is_rural, "Greens")]):
    cm = confusion_matrix(y[m], pred0[m])
    sns.heatmap(cm, annot=False, cmap=cmap, cbar=False, ax=ax, linewidths=3, linecolor="white")
    for (i, j), v in np.ndenumerate(cm):
        ax.text(j + 0.5, i + 0.5, f"{v}\n({v / cm[i].sum():.0%} of row)", ha="center", va="center",
                fontsize=11, color="white" if v > cm.max() / 2 else "#0b0b0b")
    ax.set_xticklabels(["Predicted\nnot severe", "Predicted\nsevere"]); ax.set_yticklabels(["Actually\nnot severe", "Actually\nsevere"], rotation=0)
    ax.set_title(f"{scope} (n = {m.sum()}, threshold {thr:.2f})")
plt.suptitle("Confusion matrices: every crash scored once by a model that never saw it", y=1.02, fontsize=12)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

8a. Is this the best 10? A comparison with alternatives¶

The same evaluation (identical folds, nested threshold) is run on four alternatives:

  1. All candidate features (no selection, L2-penalized).
  2. Top 10 by filter p-value alone (no first principles, no redundancy removal).
  3. The selected 10 with ILLUMINATION_DARK swapped for LEFT_TURN, the next-best by overall p-value.
  4. The selected 10.

Caveat: the selection itself used the full dataset, so the selected model's scores are slightly optimistic relative to brand-new data.

8b. Which factors matter most? Odds ratios from the final model¶

For interpretation we refit the 10-feature model on all crashes without class weights, keeping the mild L2 penalty (needed for the zero-severe flags), on the raw 0/1 features. Each odds ratio says how much the factor multiplies the odds of a severe outcome, holding the other nine fixed. The 95% intervals come from 1,000 bootstrap resamples of crashes.

Reading the protective flags: REAR_END, DEER_RELATED and DISTRACTED have zero severe crashes. Their direction is certain in this data (no bootstrap resample ever puts them above 1), but their size is set mostly by the penalty: the data alone would push them to 0. Their narrow intervals reflect the penalty, not precise knowledge. Read them as "strongly protective", not as exact values.

In [30]:
def fit_or(d):
    X = d[FINAL].astype(float).fillna(crash[FINAL].mean())
    m = LogisticRegression(C=1.0, max_iter=5000).fit(X, d[TARGET].astype(int))
    return pd.Series(np.exp(m.coef_[0]), index=FINAL)

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
point = fit_or(crash)
boot = pd.DataFrame([fit_or(crash.iloc[rng.integers(0, len(crash), len(crash))]) for _ in range(1000)])
ors = pd.DataFrame({"Odds ratio": point, "95% CI low": boot.quantile(0.025), "95% CI high": boot.quantile(0.975),
                    "% of bootstraps with OR > 1": (boot > 1).mean()}).sort_values("Odds ratio")

8c. What drives severe crashes on rural roads?¶

An odds ratio says how dangerous a factor is. How much it contributes to rural severe crashes also depends on how often it occurs on rural roads. The population attributable fraction (PAF) combines the two. Among the 11 severe rural crashes, it estimates the share that would not have been severe without the factor:

PAF = (share of severe rural crashes with the factor) × (OR − 1) / OR, for factors that raise risk (OR > 1).

With only 11 severe rural crashes these numbers are rough, but they show which factors matter in practice.

In [31]:
rs = rural_crash[rural_crash[TARGET] == 1]

                    "Severe rural crashes with factor": rs[FINAL].sum().astype(int),
                    "Share of rural crashes with factor": rural_crash[FINAL].mean()})
paf["PAF (rural)"] = np.where(paf["Odds ratio"] > 1,
                              (paf["Severe rural crashes with factor"] / len(rs)) * (paf["Odds ratio"] - 1) / paf["Odds ratio"], np.nan)
paf = paf.sort_values("PAF (rural)", ascending=False)

9. Conclusions¶

The proposed 10 features¶

Raises severity Odds ratio (95% CI) Lowers severity Odds ratio
MOTORCYCLE 4.6 (1.6–10.6) REAR_END 0.20 (0 of 127 severe)
IMPAIRED_DRIVER 2.5 (0.8–5.3) DISTRACTED 0.41 (0 of 70 severe)
SPEEDING 2.4 (0.8–6.0) DEER_RELATED 0.45 (0 of 49 severe)
DRIVER_75PLUS 1.8 (0.7–3.8) ILLUMINATION_DARK 0.55 (crash-mix effect, see 7b)
NON_COLLISION 1.8 (0.5–4.9)
AGGRESSIVE_DRIVING 1.8 (0.9–3.7)

What contributes most to fatal / serious-injury crashes on rural roads¶

  1. Aggressive driving is the biggest contributor in practice. It appears in half of all rural crashes and in 9 of the 11 severe rural crashes. By the attributable-fraction estimate, about a third of severe rural crashes are linked to it. Its effect per crash is moderate (~1.8× the odds), but it is very common.
  2. Motorcycles are the most dangerous single factor. They raise the odds ~4.6×, and in rural crashes the severe rate jumps from 6% to 50% (2 of 4). Motorcycle crashes are rare, but when one happens on a rural road the rider has no protection at highway speeds.
  3. Impairment and speeding each raise the odds ~2.4×. Both match first principles (slower reactions, more crash energy). Each accounts for roughly 10% of severe rural crashes.
  4. Drivers aged 75+ and non-collision events (rollovers, mostly single-vehicle) each raise the odds ~1.8×. Non-collision crashes are 2.8× more common on rural roads than elsewhere.
  5. What is not dangerous on rural roads: deer strikes. They are 4× more common in rural crashes (one in six), but none of the 49 was severe. Rear-ends and distraction crashes, both mostly non-rural, were also never severe. Dark-condition crashes were less severe, but because of which crashes happen in the dark (fewer motorcycles, more deer), not because darkness is safe.

How good is the model?¶

Accuracy Precision Recall F1 ROC AUC
All crashes 0.900 0.228 0.284 0.225 0.761
Rural crashes 0.898 0.322 0.413 0.304 0.841
Always predict "not severe" 0.947 0 0 0 0.5
  • Accuracy is the wrong yardstick here. A model that never predicts a severe crash scores 94.7% accuracy and catches nothing. Our model gives up some accuracy (90%) to find about 28% of severe crashes overall and ~41% on rural roads. Roughly 1 in 4 of its "severe" flags is correct, which is 4–5× better than random guessing (5%).
  • It ranks crashes well, especially on rural roads (AUC 0.84): a severe rural crash usually scores higher than a non-severe one.
  • The selected 10 beat every alternative tested. All 73 candidates: AUC 0.65, F1 0.11. The top 10 by p-value alone: AUC 0.71, F1 0.16. This supports combining first principles with the filter rather than relying on statistics alone.

Limitations: read these before acting on the results¶

  • Very few severe crashes: 36 in total and only 11 on rural roads. Only MOTORCYCLE has an interval that clearly excludes "no effect"; AGGRESSIVE_DRIVING and IMPAIRED_DRIVER are borderline. Rural metrics swing widely between folds (F1 ± 0.25).
  • Slightly optimistic scores: the features were chosen using the full dataset, so performance on brand-new data will probably be a little lower.
  • Association, not causation, especially for darkness (section 7b) and the zero-severe flags.
  • Important variables are missing from this extract: seat-belt use, curves, head-on risk on undivided two-lane roads, and distance to a trauma center. First principles and the wider literature rank these among the main rural severity factors.
  • Data cleaning mattered: 30% of the rows were duplicate records of the same crash (one per road involved). Without collapsing them, the model would be tested on crashes it had already seen.

Next step: repeat this analysis on several years of PennDOT data (thousands of rural severe crashes). Include UNBELTED, CURVED_ROAD and HO_OPPDIR_SDSWP, and fit a rural-only model to confirm these factors.
